hook.text: Hunger isn't just willpower. It's a conversation between your gut and your brain, and GLP-1 medications change that conversation.

gut.text: After you eat, special cells in your gut release a hormone called GLP-1. It travels through the blood to tell your brain: you're full.

brain.text: In the hypothalamus, the brain's appetite center, GLP-1 switches on fullness neurons and quiets hunger neurons. It also turns down the reward signals behind cravings.

stomach.text: It also slows how quickly the stomach empties, so you feel full for longer. That's also why nausea is a common side effect.

lasting.text: The catch: natural GLP-1 is broken down within minutes. These medications are engineered to last for days, so the fullness signal stays on.

type1.text: There are three types. The first, a single agonist, activates only the GLP-1 receptor.

type2.text: The second, a dual agonist, also activates the receptor for a second gut hormone called GIP, which may add appetite effects and help tolerability.

type3.text: The third, a triple agonist, adds the glucagon receptor, which may increase energy use. This type is research only right now. It is not approved for use.

beema.text: Beema Health does not sell the third type. Beema Health offers only compounded medications in the first two categories. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved, and a licensed provider decides whether any treatment is appropriate.
